414.title: Call Him by His names
414.hook: the beautiful names again, in their home verse (7:180)
414.howItsDone: Muslims often begin a du'a with the divine name that fits the request, such as ya Razzaq for provision or ya Ghafur for forgiveness, and some learn the ninety-nine names by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mithaq, the covenant of Alast. Your line was we said yes. Today, the beautiful names come back, in the verse they call home.

On day two hundred thirty-two, this path opened the most beautiful names of Allah with the first half of this verse: the Merciful, the Forgiving, the Provider, the Patient. Lists of names are lovely to read, and easy to treat like a museum, beautiful things behind glass. Today, the verse again, read all the way through, in its place in surah seven. It says what the names are for, and then how they can be bent.
screen: `DAY 232, THE FIRST HALF.` → `NAMES BEHIND GLASS?` → `WHAT THEY'RE FOR.`

segments.voice: Verse one-eighty, in Pickthall's words: “Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them.” In Arabic: wa lillahi al-asma' al-husna, fad'uhu biha. The word for call, ud'u, shares a root with du'a. The names aren't only to know. They're to use, the way you use someone's name to get their attention. So scholars teach matching the name to the need: when you need provision, ar-Razzaq, the Provider; when you've done wrong, al-Ghafur, the Forgiving; when you're afraid, as-Salam, Peace. The verse goes on: leave those who distort His names. The verb is yulhiduna, from a root meaning to swerve to one side. A Muslim grave may have a lahd, a niche dug into the side wall: the same root. To distort the names is to bend them away from what they mean. How many are there? A hadith in Bukhari says Allah has ninety-nine names, and whoever counts them will enter paradise; scholars explained count as learning, understanding and living by them. But some scholars held that ninety-nine is not the limit, citing a du'a reported from the Prophet ﷺ that asks by every name Allah has named Himself, including those He kept hidden with Himself. The list is a door, not the whole house. The phrase al-asma' al-husna appears in four places in the Qur'an. Here it comes with a plain command, and a warning.

segments.voice: Name to yourself one thing you need today, plainly: patience with a child, money for rent, courage for a conversation, rest. Pick the name that fits it, the Patient, the Provider, the Strong, Peace. If you pray, call on Him by that name quietly, a few times with the breath; if you don't, sit with the name and the need side by side.
Al-asma' al-husna, the most beautiful names. Surah seven, verse one-eighty: to Allah belong them, so call on Him by them.

415.title: When it is recited, listen
415.hook: when the Qur'an is recited, listen and be silent (7:204–205)
415.howItsDone: Muslims listen to Qur'an recitation in silence, at home, in the mosque and on the radio; at 7:206, the first prostration verse in the mushaf, reciters and listeners traditionally make a prostration of recitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-asma' al-husna, call Him by His names. Your line was the names are for calling. Today, the last verses of surah seven, and an instruction about your ears.
screen: `AL-ASMA' AL-HUSNA — THE NAMES ARE FOR CALLING.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once asked a companion, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, to recite the Qur'an to him. Ibn Mas'ud was surprised: recite it to you, when it was revealed to you? The Prophet said he loved to hear it from someone else. So Ibn Mas'ud began surah four, the Women. When he reached a verse about the Day when each community brings a witness, the Prophet said, enough. Ibn Mas'ud looked up and saw his eyes full of tears. The one who brought the Qur'an, listening to it, in silence.
screen: `RECITE IT TO ME.` → `I LOVE TO HEAR IT FROM ANOTHER.` → `HIS EYES FULL OF TEARS.`

segments.voice: Surah seven ends with three verses that begin with that kind of listening. Verse two-oh-four, in Pickthall's words: “And when the Qur'an is recited, give ear to it and pay heed, that ye may obtain mercy.” Two Arabic verbs. Istami'u: listen closely, lean in with your hearing. Ansitu: be silent, the silence of someone paying attention, not merely not talking. In Mecca, surah forty-one reports, some opponents told each other to make noise whenever the Qur'an was recited, to drown it out. This verse asks for the opposite. Jurists also debated what it means in congregational prayer. Hanafi scholars say the one praying behind an imam should stay silent while he recites, citing this verse. Shafi'i scholars hold that each person still recites al-Fatiha quietly, citing a hadith. Both take the verse seriously; they differ on how it applies. Verse two-oh-five continues: remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with awe, below the voice, morning and evening, and don't be among the heedless. And the last verse, two-oh-six, says those near your Lord are not too proud to worship Him; they glorify Him and prostrate to Him. In the order of the mushaf, it's the first of the verses at which reciters and listeners traditionally bow down in prostration. So al-A'raf ends here: ears open, voice low, forehead on the ground.

segments.voice: Play a short recitation at a low volume, any reciter, any surah, or sit in silence and recall one you've heard, or simply listen to the room. Don't follow along on a screen or try to translate; just listen, the way the Prophet listened to Ibn Mas'ud, still and open, letting the sound arrive.

Your line: listen, be still. And with that, surah seven, the Heights, is finished. Until tomorrow.

416.title: Hearts that tremble
416.hook: believers are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned (8:2)
416.howItsDone: Muslims read 8:2–4 as a portrait of the believer; many scholars cite 8:2 to teach that faith increases and decreases, and recitation is valued for moving the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ansitu, when it is recited, listen, and surah seven ended in prostration. Your line was listen, be still. Today, surah eight, and a heart that moves when it hears.

Surah eight is al-Anfal, the Spoils, revealed in Medina after the battle of Badr, in the second year after the emigration: the first major clash between the young Muslim community and the Quraysh of Mecca. It opens on an awkward note. Right after the battle, the companions are arguing over the spoils, who gets what, who earned more. The first verse says the spoils belong to Allah and the messenger, so be mindful, and set things right between you. Then the second verse turns from what's in their hands to what's in their hearts.
screen: `AL-ANFAL — THE SPOILS.` → `AFTER BADR, AN ARGUMENT.` → `FROM THE HANDS TO THE HEARTS.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “They only are the (true) believers whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned.” The verb is wajilat: their hearts tremble, quake, shiver with awe. Pickthall says fear, and the early commentators kept that sense: al-Suddi pictured a man about to do wrong who is told, fear God, and his heart trembles, and he stops. But the word holds awe as well, the shiver at the edge of something enormous. The verse goes on: when His verses are recited to them, their faith increases, and they put their trust in their Lord. Then verse three: they establish the prayer and spend from what We've given them. Notice the order: a heart that moves, faith that grows, trust, then prayer and giving. The outward follows the inward. And faith can increase; many scholars took this verse as evidence that faith isn't a fixed amount, but rises and falls. Here's a puzzle, though. Surah thirteen says that in the remembrance of Allah, hearts find rest. So which is it, trembling or rest? Commentators answered: both. Surah thirty-nine says it in one breath: skins shiver at the recitation, then skins and hearts soften toward the remembrance of Allah. First the shiver, then the softening. A heart that never trembles at anything might be calm, or simply numb. Coming right after a quarrel over spoils, these verses seem to say: if the heart is moved by the right thing, the hands will stop grabbing.

segments.voice: Think back over the last month to a time your heart actually moved: a piece of music, a child's laugh, a verse, a funeral, a sunrise, a stranger's kindness. Remember it in detail until you feel even a faint echo of it now, notice where that feeling lives in your body, and rest there.
Wajilat, trembles, shivers with awe. The believers whose hearts do this at the mention of Allah, and whose faith grows. Today's word.

417.title: You did not throw
417.hook: at Badr, you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw (8:17)
417.tomorrow: Between a man and his heart
417.howItsDone: Muslims often answer praise or good news with alhamdulillah or ma sha' Allah, and teachers cite 8:17 to explain why success is credited to Allah while effort is still expected.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wajilat, hearts that tremble. Your line was a heart that trembles. Today, still at Badr, a verse about who gets the credit.

An award show. The winner reaches the microphone and starts thanking people: my coach, my mom, the team, the crew. Some of it is politeness. But often there's something true in it: the trophy has their name on it, and it was never only them. At Badr, the sources say, the Muslims were badly outnumbered. Commentators report that as the battle began, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ picked up a handful of pebbles and dust and threw it toward the other army. Afterward, a verse came about that throw.
screen: `THE ACCEPTANCE SPEECH.` → `OUTNUMBERED AT BADR.` → `A HANDFUL OF PEBBLES.`

segments.voice: Verse seventeen begins with the believers: you did not slay them, but Allah slew them. Then it turns to the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: “thou (Muhammad) threwest not when thou didst throw, but Allah threw.” In Arabic it's almost a riddle: wa ma ramayta idh ramayta, wa lakinna Allaha rama. You did not throw, when you threw. The verse doesn't deny that the Prophet's arm moved. It says you threw, and in the same breath, it wasn't you. In the verse's telling, both are true at once: the hand was his; the reaching of that handful, and what came of it, was Allah's. The verse goes on: that He might test the believers with a good test from Him. Even victory is a test. Will you say, look at us? The surah opened with an argument over the spoils, and this verse quietly answers it: if the win wasn't only yours, the spoils aren't only yours either. Muslim theologians have long argued over how a human act can be both truly yours and truly from God; different schools gave different answers, and the debate is still taught. The everyday lesson teachers draw is simpler. Effort is real, and it matters. Success is a gift, and it humbles. After good news, a job, a grade, a recovery, Muslims say alhamdulillah, praise be to God. In a way, it's this verse in one word.
screen: `WA MA RAMAYTA — YOU DID NOT THROW.` · `THE HAND WAS HIS; THE REST, ALLAH'S.` · `EVEN VICTORY IS A TEST.` · `EFFORT REAL, SUCCESS A GIFT.` · then, large: `BUT ALLAH THREW.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're proud of from this week or this year, and let yourself feel the effort you put in, because it was real. Then widen the picture: the health that let you do it, the people who taught you, the timing you didn't control, the breath in your lungs. If you pray, say alhamdulillah for it; if not, simply credit what wasn't you.

Your line: it wasn't only me. The effort was real, and so was the gift. That's day four hundred seventeen.

418.title: Between a man and his heart
418.hook: Allah comes between a person and his heart (8:24)
418.carry: he is nearer than my heart
418.howItsDone: Muslims repeat the Prophet's du'a, ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik (O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion), especially in hard or uncertain times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rama, you did not throw. Your line was it wasn't only me. Today, from the hand to the heart, and a verse that goes closer than anything.

Pick up an old diary, and the person who wrote it can seem like a stranger: in love with things since dropped, afraid of things that never came, sure of plans that now look foolish. Hearts change. In Arabic the heart is qalb, and the same root gives the word for turning: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called God muqallib al-qulub, the Turner of hearts. Surah eight has a verse about who stands at that turning point.
screen: `AN OLD DIARY, A STRANGER.` → `QALB — THE THING THAT TURNS.` → `WHO STANDS AT THE TURNING?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-four opens with an invitation: O you who believe, respond to Allah and the messenger when he calls you to what gives you life. Then, in Pickthall's words: “know that Allah cometh in between the man and his own heart,” and that to Him you will be gathered. What does that mean? Early commentators gave two readings, and both are still taught. One: Allah is closer to a person than their own heart. Surah fifty says He is nearer than the vein in their neck. The heart is the most inward thing a person has, and He is nearer still. Two: Allah can turn a heart. He can stand between a person and what their heart wants, or the faith they assumed they'd always have. So, the verse implies, respond while your heart is open; don't assume you'll feel the same next year. That second reading sits behind a du'a the Prophet is reported to have said often. In Tirmidhi's collection, his wife Umm Salamah says it was the du'a he made most: ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik. O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion. Asked why, he said every heart is held between two fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns it as He wills. That's a man whose heart his followers trusted completely, asking for steadiness, every day. The heart is not a fortress. It's a door on a hinge, and the verse says who holds the hinge.

419.title: Don't quarrel
419.hook: don't dispute, or you'll lose heart and your strength will go (8:46)
419.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 8:46 when calling communities, families and mosque committees to unity, and distinguish respectful scholarly difference (ikhtilaf) from divisive quarreling (tanazu').

segments.voice: Yesterday: muqallib al-qulub, the Turner of hearts, and your line, he is nearer than my heart. Today, what happens between people when hearts pull in different directions.
screen: `MUQALLIB AL-QULUB — HE IS NEARER THAN MY HEART.`

segments.voice: A sailboat with two people at the helm, each pulling the tiller their own way, goes nowhere. The sail flaps. The boat turns in circles. Everyone works hard, and all the work cancels out. Families do this. Teams do this. Whole communities do it, over things that look enormous at the time and tiny ten years later. Surah eight remembers a community that had just come through Badr, and would learn at Uhud what quarreling costs. Its verse forty-six uses the image of wind.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE AT THE TILLER.` → `THE SAIL FLAPS.` → `AN IMAGE OF WIND.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you; but be steadfast!” The verse adds: Allah is with the steadfast. The Arabic word for dispute is tanaza'u, from a root that means to pull, to snatch: two people tugging the same rope in opposite directions. It's not ordinary disagreement. Companions disagreed about strategy, meanings and rulings, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at times let the difference stand. Tanazu' is disagreement turned into a tug-of-war. The result: fa-tafshalu, you'll lose heart, go slack, fail. And tadhhaba rihukum. Pickthall has your strength will depart; literally, your wind will go. In Arabic, a person's wind can mean their power, their momentum, the way English says the wind went out of their sails. Some early commentators also took it more literally: the wind of help that blows for a people at their best. Surah three, looking back on Uhud, describes what happened: a group lost heart, disputed over the order they'd been given, and disobeyed, and the day turned. The archers argued over whether to hold their post on the hill, and many left it. So surah eight is naming a pattern the community would learn the hard way. Its answer isn't never disagree. It's sabr: steadiness. Stay at your post. Hold your tongue when the argument has turned into tugging. Allah is with the steady ones.

420.title: If they incline to peace
420.hook: if they incline to peace, incline to it too, and trust in Allah (8:61)
420.howItsDone: Muslim jurists cite 8:61 for accepting genuine offers of peace and truce, and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah is taught as its classic example; Muslims also apply it to quarrels between family and friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't quarrel, and your line, quarrels weaken. A week ends today: the names, the listening, the trembling heart, the throw, the hinge of the heart, the quarrel. Now, peace.

A long argument, and then the other person says, quietly, okay, can we stop? It's often not a full apology. Sometimes it's just a cup of tea set down in front of you, or a text with a joke in it. And in that moment, there's a choice. You can say, not until you admit you were wrong. Or you can take the tea. Surah eight was revealed in wartime, between real enemies, about real treaties. And near its end it gives a rule for that exact moment.
screen: `OKAY, CAN WE STOP?` → `A CUP OF TEA SET DOWN.` → `A RULE FOR THAT MOMENT.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “And if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it, and trust in Allah.” The verb is janaha. Its root gives the Arabic word for a wing, janah. To incline is to lean, the way a bird tips its wing as it turns. If they lean toward peace, lean toward it too. The word for peace here is silm, from the same root as salam, and as islam. The next verse meets the obvious worry: what if it's a trick? And if they mean to deceive you, Allah is enough for you. The risk of being fooled is not a reason to refuse an honest-looking offer. Later, at a place called Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ agreed to a treaty with Quraysh whose terms some of his companions found hard to swallow. They were turned back from Mecca that year, and some of the conditions looked one-sided. He accepted. A surah revealed on the way home calls it a clear victory, and early historians report that in the peace that followed, more people came to Islam than in the years of fighting. Scholars have debated how this verse sits beside harder verses in the next surah. Some early scholars said those later verses replaced it. Others, including al-Tabari, held that it still stands, and that peace is to be accepted when it is truly offered. A few verses later, surah eight, the Spoils, ends with the bonds between believers who stood by each other.
